```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.


Data Exploration
# The mtcars dataset is built into R -- no import needed.
data(mtcars)
# TODO: Use head() to display the first 6 rows of mtcars
# TODO: Use str() to show the structure (column types) of mtcars

```{r}
data(mtcars)
head(mtcars)
str(mtcars)
```

Question: How many observations (rows) and variables (columns) does mtcars have?

Answer:The mtcars dataset has 32 observations (rows) and 11 variables (columns).

# TODO: Use summary() to get summary statistics for the whole dataset
# TODO: Calculate the average mpg for each value of cyl (4, 6, 8 cylinders)
# Hint: use aggregate(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars, FUN = mean)

```{r}
summary(mtcars)
aggregate(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars, FUN = mean)
```

Question: Which cylinder group has the highest average mpg? Does this match your prediction above?

Answer:The 4-cylinder group has the highest average fuel efficiency, with about 26.66 mpg. Yes, this matches my prediction because cars with fewer cylinders generally have better fuel efficiency.

# TODO: Create a scatterplot of mpg (y-axis) vs. wt (x-axis)
# Hint: plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg,
#            xlab = "Weight (1000 lbs)", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
#            main = "Fuel Efficiency vs. Weight")
# TODO: Create a boxplot of mpg grouped by cyl
# Hint: boxplot(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars,
#               xlab = "Number of Cylinders", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
#               main = "Fuel Efficiency by Cylinder Count")
```{r}
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg,
     xlab = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
     ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Fuel Efficiency vs. Weight")
```

```{r}
boxplot(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars,
        xlab = "Number of Cylinders",
        ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
        main = "Fuel Efficiency by Cylinder Count")
```

Question: Based on the scatterplot, describe the relationship between a car’s weight and its fuel efficiency.

Answer:Based on the scatterplot, heavier cars usually have lower fuel efficiency. As the weight of a car increases, its mpg tends to decrease. This means lighter cars generally use fuel more efficiently than heavier cars.


Conclusion:From this activity, I learned that a car's weight and number of cylinders can affect its fuel efficiency. Cars with fewer cylinders usually have higher mpg, while cars with more cylinders tend to have lower mpg. I also noticed that heavier cars generally have lower fuel efficiency than lighter cars. Overall, lighter cars with fewer cylinders tend to be more fuel-efficient in this dataset.
